chunks: From him, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from al-Qasim ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Eat the slaughtered meat of the polytheists if they mention the name of Allah upon it while you hear it, and do not eat the slaughtered meat of the Arab Christians.

key_terms.الْعَرَبِ: The Arabs (specifically Arab Christians in this context)
key_terms.الْمُشْرِكِينَ: Polytheists (those who associate partners with God)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling between eating the meat of polytheists and Arab Christians in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahar highlights the juristic distinction between general polytheists and Arab Christians, a key topic in Shia fiqh regarding the purity of their slaughtered animals. While the invocation of Allah's name validates the meat of polytheists, the specific prohibition of Arab Christians reflects their unique status as 'People of the Book' with distinct ritual practices. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the specific conditions of slaughter and the theological categorization of different non-Muslim groups.
